summary: Proposes TCP extensions for efficient operation over paths with a high bandwidth-delay product, such as satellite links. They were meant as a basis for experiments and research, not an Internet standard. It is historic, replaced by RFC 1323, RFC 2018 and RFC 6247.

plainLanguage.summary: When a path is long and fast, a sender can wait a long time for replies. These changes let it keep many packets in flight.

questions: what are tcp extensions for long delay paths
how did tcp handle high bandwidth delay product
what is window scaling in tcp
what is the tcp echo option
subtitle: Options for protocols working over satellite and long-distance paths.

tldr.problem: On paths with high bandwidth and long delays, such as satellite links, TCP's 16-bit window and simple acknowledgment scheme make it impossible to keep the link full, wasting bandwidth.
tldr.mechanism: Three new TCP options allow window scaling up to 1 gigabyte, selective acknowledgment of received segments, and timestamp measurement to improve round-trip time estimates.
tldr.outcome: These extensions were meant for research only, not as an Internet standard. They form the basis of later standards RFC 1323 (Windows and Timestamps), RFC 2018 (SACK), and RFC 6247 (consolidation).

today: RFC 1072 is Historic and no longer a standard. It was replaced by RFC 1323 (TCP Extensions for High Performance), RFC 2018 (TCP Selective Acknowledgment Options), and RFC 6247 (TCP Window Scaling and Timestamps Obsolete Documentation). While the original proposed options are no longer the standard forms, the core ideas—window scaling, SACK, and timestamp-based RTT measurement—are now part of modern TCP and are widely deployed.

sections.title: The Problem: Long, Fat Pipes
sections.content:
The RFC introduces the concept of a high bandwidth-delay product, or long, fat pipe (LFN), where the product of bandwidth in bits per second and round-trip delay in seconds exceeds 10 to the 5th power bits. This is the amount of data that must be in flight to fill the network pipe. For example, a T1-speed satellite channel with a bandwidth-delay product over 10 to the 6th power bits can require 100 outstanding TCP segments of 1,200 bytes each.

TCP was designed for small, fast paths. Its 16-bit window field limits unacknowledged data to 65 kilobytes. When you need more data in flight to fill a gigabit or satellite pipe, TCP cannot keep up. Clever algorithms alone cannot fix this; the protocol itself must be extended.
sections.plainLanguage: TCP was invented for short, slow networks. On satellite links or across oceans, the delay is so long that TCP runs out of window before hearing back, so it sits idle instead of keeping packets flowing.

sections.title: Three Fundamental Problems
sections.content:
The RFC identifies three problems that prevent good TCP performance on LFN paths.

First, window size limitation: the TCP header uses a 16-bit field for the receive window, capping it at 65,535 bytes. This is far too small for paths that need gigabytes of data in flight.

Second, cumulative acknowledgments: when a segment is lost among many in flight, TCP has no way to tell the sender which of the succeeding segments arrived safely. The sender must retransmit everything from the lost one onward, wasting bandwidth.

Third, poor round-trip timing: measuring RTT requires timing individual segments. Some implementations time only one segment per window to save CPU. On an LFN with 100 segments in the window, this gives a useless RTT estimate. Retransmissions make it worse: you cannot reliably time a segment that has been retransmitted because the ACK might belong to the first or second transmission.
sections.plainLanguage: TCP has three weak points on long pipes. It cannot send enough data at once. If one packet is lost, it has to resend lots of good packets too. And it cannot measure delays accurately because there are so many packets in flight.

sections.title: The Solutions: Three New TCP Options
sections.content:
The RFC proposes three new TCP options that can be negotiated during connection setup. Each addresses one of the three problems.

The Window Scale option allows both sides to agree on a scale factor that multiplies the window field value. If scale is 7, a window of 65,535 becomes 65,535 × 128 = 8,388,480 bytes. The scale factor is communicated in the TCP SYN segment and cannot change during the connection.

The SACK-permitted option signals that selective acknowledgments may be used. Once enabled, a receiver can send a SACK option listing which blocks of data have arrived out of order, telling the sender exactly which segments need to be resent.

The TCP Echo and Echo Reply options let a sender put a timestamp or other value in each segment, and the receiver echoes it back in the ACK. This allows the sender to measure the RTT of every segment, including retransmissions, with negligible CPU cost.
sections.plainLanguage: To fix these three problems, the RFC adds three tools: a way to say "multiply my window by 128 to get the real size," a way to say "I got these packets, but not that one," and a way for each packet to carry a timestamp so the sender knows how long it took.

sections.title: Window Scaling
sections.content:
Window scaling works by encoding a shift count in a three-byte TCP option sent in the SYN segment. The shift count is a power of 2 applied via binary shift. A shift count of 1 means left-shift by 1 (multiply by 2), a shift count of 7 means left-shift by 7 (multiply by 128).

The option is an offer, not a promise. Both sides must send a Window Scale option in their SYN segments for scaling to work in either direction. If one side does not offer it, normal 16-bit windows are used.

The maximum shift count is limited to 14, yielding a maximum window of 2 to the 30th power bytes (1 gigabyte). This limit ensures that TCP can still distinguish old data from new data in its sequence number space.
sections.plainLanguage: Window scaling is like an agreement to read the window number in a different way. Instead of "65,535 bytes," you agree to read it as "65,535 times 2-to-the-7, or about 8 million bytes."

sections.title: Selective Acknowledgment (SACK)
sections.content:
SACK uses two options. The SACK-permitted option in a SYN segment signals that the connection may use SACK. Once permitted, the receiver can send a SACK option in any data segment it originates.

A SACK option lists the blocks of contiguous sequence space that have been received and queued, using Relative Origin (first byte relative to the current ACK number) and Block Size (octets in the block). Up to 10 blocks fit in the 44 bytes of TCP option space. The ACK number still indicates the left edge of the window (the first unacknowledged byte), so a SACK is advisory: if ignored, TCP works as before.

When window scaling is in use, SACK fields are scaled by the same factor as the window to preserve precision. This means blocks must be reported as multiples of the scale factor, introducing small loss of precision, but the sender can usually infer the real segment boundaries from its retransmission queue.
sections.plainLanguage: Selective acknowledgment lets the receiver tell the sender, "I got bytes 500 through 999 and bytes 1500 through 1999, but not the bytes in between." The sender then resends only the missing piece, not everything from the gap onward.

sections.title: Echo Options for Round-Trip Timing
sections.content:
The RFC proposes a TCP Echo option (option 6) carrying 4 bytes of data, and a TCP Echo Reply option (option 7) that echoes back the same 4 bytes. A sender can include the Echo option in any segment, but only if the receiver's SYN contained an Echo option.

When used for RTT measurement, the 4 bytes hold a timestamp in any format the sender chooses. The receiver echoes the timestamp in the next segment it sends (an ACK, or data). If multiple Echo options arrive before a reply segment is sent, the receiver chooses the newest segment with the oldest sequence number, balancing the need to time the oldest unacknowledged data (for delayed ACK) while preferring recent measurements.

This approach avoids the retransmission ambiguity that makes simple ACK-based RTT measurement unreliable: the timestamp is carried with the segment, so the sender knows which flight of transmission the echo measures.
sections.plainLanguage: Each packet can carry a timestamp in 4 bytes. When the other side sends an ACK back, it copies that timestamp. The sender reads the current time and sees how long the round trip took, even for packets that had to be sent twice.
